newsitem.title: USA: Chicken with altered brain sings like a quail.
newsitem.headline: Chicken with altered brain sings like a quail.

text.p: In a study providing insight into the complex workings of the brain, a researcher said on Tuesday he was able to make a baby chicken sing like a quail by transplanting brain parts from the quail into the chicken.

Evan Balaban, a neurobiologist at the La Jolla, California-based Neurosciences Institute, also said he was able to isolate different components of the quail's song, such as the sound and the accompanying head movement, so one or both activities could be transferred into the chicken.
The findings were published on Tuesday in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

"We are trying to get a much finer understanding of how cell differences are correlated with behavioural performance," said Balaban. "If we understand what brain cells make a difference in behavioural circuits, it could lead the way for trying to alter some features of those cells."
Balaban said the study showed the baby chickens did not simply learn how to sing from their parents but got a signal from the brain.

Although the idea of mixing and matching parts of different species raises the specter of all sorts of cross breeding, Balaban said that was not the purpose of his experiment. In fact, he said, such research would not be possible in humans or most other mammals.
"In mammals it is simply not possible to have access," to the brain in such a young embryo, he said.

But he said the research does help to explain the intricate ways different brain parts develop and work in unison. At some future point, he said it could be used to develop better treatments for human brain damage. Knowledge on what parts of the brain contribute to different behaviours is currently sparse.

In the chicken embryos, Balaban said he was interested in taking a relatively complex behaviour, like singing, and seeing if he could determine how many parts of the brain had to be changed to affect the behaviour.

He determined that two parts of the brain, the brain stem and the mid-brain section, had to be changed to get the chicken to sing like a quail. The corresponding brain parts from a quail were transplanted into a two-day-old chicken embryo, whose song was observed shortly after hatching.

A chicken's song is a short squeak accompanied by a forward and back head motion, while a quail, Balaban said, sings three distinct sounds and shakes its head up and down rapidly. But in another sign of the complexity of brain function, the chicken with the altered brain continued to yawn like a regular chicken after adopting other head movements of the quail.
